readerTitle: Why a café turns down beans that are 10% cheaper
caseNote: 가상 사례 (카페와 원두 공급사, 미용실 예약 소프트웨어) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 고객을 지키는 것은 가격이 아니라 떠날 때 치러야 하는 비용이다. 경쟁사의 할인은 그 비용보다 클 때만 고객을 움직인다.
misconception: 더 싸고 품질이 같으면 고객은 바로 옮겨 간다. 고객을 붙잡으려면 계약과 위약금으로 묶어 두면 된다.

sources.text: 경쟁 전략의 표준 개념 (전환 비용, 해자로서의 고객 고착)

factChecks.note: 전환 비용 계산: 에스프레소 머신 구입 $6,000 + 바리스타 재교육 3명 × 6시간 × 시급 $20 = $360 + 그라인더 세팅·시험 추출용 원두 $300 = $6,660.
공급사가 머신을 무상 대여하는 방식은 원두 업계에서 흔한 계약 형태로 일반적으로 설명했습니다. 특정 기업이나 업계 통계는 인용하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why a café turns down beans that are 10% cheaper
body: A café spends $1,000 a month on coffee beans. A new roaster offers the same quality for 10% less.
The owner says no, without even tasting a sample. She isn't being careless. She has done the math, and the price is the smallest number in it.

image.label: Café owner declining a cheaper bag of beans
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 카페 카운터에서 주인이 "-10%" 태그가 붙은 원두 봉투를 정중히 손으로 밀어내는 장면. 뒤에는 큰 에스프레소 머신. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You're the new roaster. She said no.
body: Her current roaster lends her the espresso machine for free, as long as she buys their beans. Her baristas are trained on that roaster's blend and settings.
You want her business. What do you offer?

options.text: Cut your price to 20% below her current roaster
options.feedback: You give up a lot of margin on every bag, and she may still say no. A bigger discount only works if it outweighs what leaving costs her.

options.text: Lend her a machine and train her staff for free
options.feedback: You pay down the cost of leaving instead of fighting on price. It costs you money upfront, but it removes the real reason she stays.

options.text: Send free samples to prove your beans taste better
options.feedback: Quality helps, and she may like your beans. But she already believed they were good. Taste wasn't what kept her.

cards.title: What leaving would cost her.
body: The cheaper beans save **$1,200 a year**. Leaving costs $6,660 on day one. She would need about 5.5 years just to break even, and that ignores the risk that regulars notice a different taste.

cards.title: Switching costs
body: **Switching costs** are everything a customer must spend, learn, risk or give up to move to a rival.
When they are high, a business can keep customers even if a competitor is a bit cheaper or a bit better. That makes switching costs a moat: a protection that rivals can't easily cross.
The old roaster isn't winning on beans. It's winning on the machine and the habits built around it.

image.label: A customer facing a wall of costs between two shops
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 가게에서 오른쪽 가게로 가는 길 사이에 벽돌 벽이 있고, 벽돌마다 "Machine", "Training", "Test batches", "Risk" 라벨. 오른쪽 가게 앞의 "-10%" 표지판은 작게.

cards.title: How big a discount would it take?
body: Years it takes the café to earn back $6,660, at different discounts on $12,000 of beans a year.
Even a 30% price cut needs almost two years to pay off. Rivals can rarely give up that much margin for long.

cards.title: Switching costs come in four kinds.
body: Most businesses have more than one, and they add up.
list: **Effort:** learning a new system, moving records, retraining staff
**Risk:** will the new option work as well, and who gets blamed if it doesn't
**Loss:** rewards, history or relationships left behind
cards.callout: Ask which of these your customers would face. That's the size of your moat.
cards.softwareNote: In software, effort and loss are often the biggest: years of stored data, connected tools and staff who know where every button is.

cards.title: Trapped customers are not loyal customers.
body: Switching costs that come from real value, like stored history or tools that fit a workflow, keep customers happy. Switching costs that feel like a trap, like exit fees or locked data, breed resentment. Those customers leave the day they can and warn others.
They also shrink. Contracts end, equipment wears out, and a rival can pay the cost for the customer, as the new roaster could. Use the headroom to serve customers better, not to squeeze them.

image.label: A door held shut by a chain versus a cozy room
image.brief: 두 장면 나란히. 왼쪽은 쇠사슬로 잠긴 문 앞에서 불만스러운 고객, 오른쪽은 자기 물건과 기록이 정리된 편안한 방에 머무는 고객. 대비가 분명하게.

cards.title: Now it's salon booking software.
body: You sell booking software to hair salons. A rival launches at 30% less. You want salons to stay without resenting you.

options.text: Move everyone to two-year contracts with an exit fee
options.feedback: It buys time, but the cost of leaving disappears at renewal, and salons remember being boxed in.

options.text: Build client history, color notes and reminders salons rely on every day
options.feedback: Leaving now means losing records stylists use with every client. The cost of switching grows because the product is useful, not because users are trapped.

options.text: Make it hard to export client data
options.feedback: It may slow a few departures. But salons feel held hostage, word spreads among owners, and rivals will advertise easy imports.

cards.title: Customers stay when leaving costs more than staying.
body: A rival's discount only wins if it beats the money, effort, risk and loss of switching. Build those costs through value, and you can compete on more than price.
**Try it today:** list what a customer would have to spend, learn, risk or give up to leave you. Then ask which of those they'd thank you for.
